book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

clue.text: It shows pressure or bias is developing

indicators.note: something developing is still taking shape, so the letters before it are not yet in their final order

parts.note: the two words supply the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sign that some pressure group's prejudice is starting to show.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobar is a line on a weather map joining places of equal atmospheric pressure, so it shows the pressure pattern.

clue.text: In fine form it is immeasurable

indicators.note: to form is to shape, so the letters are shaped into a new word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: When something is in excellent shape its worth cannot be measured.
explanation.definitionFit: Something infinite is without limits, too great to be measured.

clue.text: Out when ball hit to leg

parts.note: in cricket, the on side is the leg side
a strike is a hit, and in bowling one ball that fells every pin

explanation.surface: A batsman is dismissed after the ball strikes him on the leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Out is not a cricket dismissal here but workers out on a picket line. On side is cricket's name for the leg side of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers who are out have withdrawn their labour, which is to say they have stopped work in protest.

clue.text: A study of foreign capital

parts.note: taken as written
a den is a private study

explanation.surface: An academic paper examining overseas investment.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital looks financial; it is a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Aden was the capital of South Yemen and remains a major Yemeni port city.

clue.text: Subtle meaning — but also an obvious one
Suitable fruit for queen of puddings?

definitions.text: Suitable fruit for queen of puddings?

parts.words: Suitable fruit for queen of puddings?
parts.note: surface reading: a fruit to go in the classic custard and meringue dessert
setter's reading: a fruit named after a queen would suit a queen's pudding

explanation.walkthrough: Queen of puddings is a British baked dessert of breadcrumb custard topped with jam and meringue; the fruit wanted bears a famous queen's name.
explanation.definitionFit: This English plum variety is named after Queen Victoria, so it is the royal fruit for a royal pudding.

clue.text: It can be raised for getting upset about nothing

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so in a down clue the word is turned upside down
about means around, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A temper can flare when someone gets upset over trifles.
explanation.walkthrough: To raise the roof is to make a great noise; to hit the roof is to get angry, which the surface hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: A roof can be raised in the idiom raise the roof, meaning to cheer or shout very loudly.

clue.text: Admitting being the proprietor?

explanation.surface: Confessing that you are the owner of the business.
explanation.definitionFit: To own to something is to confess it, and to own is to possess, so the participle carries both.

clue.text: Noted mistakes in Latin

parts.note: surface reading: famous blunders in a Latin text
setter's reading: errors written down in a list, the word itself being Latin

explanation.walkthrough: Noted suggests famous; it means written down, and in Latin says what language the word comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata is the Latin plural for errors, used for a printed list of corrections in a book.

clue.text: Fan set out for tie

indicators.note: set out suggests things laid out afresh, so the letters are spread and rearranged

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A football supporter lays out a club tie ready to wear.
explanation.definitionFit: To fasten something is to secure or bind it, the verb sense of tie.

clue.text: No chores undone in this vessel

indicators.note: something undone has been taken apart, so the letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: On this boat nobody does the housework.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is a sailing ship with two or more masts, a kind of vessel.

clue.text: Contemplating truancy?

parts.note: surface reading: a pupil thinking about skipping school
setter's reading: the mind itself is the thing that goes missing

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words: a mind that is absent, playing truant.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone forgetful and preoccupied has a wandering mind, as if their thoughts were away from class.

clue.text: Usual amount and not a large number

parts.note: nor means and not
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A normal quantity, and certainly not a huge one.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is the standard or typical level, such as the expected quantity of work or output.

clue.text: Regard sailor with horror? Not half!

definitions.note: the definition is regard with horror, with sailor sitting inside it

indicators.note: not half asks for only half the word, so its second half is dropped

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor
taken as written before cutting

explanation.surface: Does one view a seaman with dread? Not half, meaning very much so.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition, regard with horror, wraps around the word sailor. Not half! is also British slang for 'absolutely'.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor something is to detest it, to look on it with loathing.

clue.text: Body of soldiers almost close ranks

indicators.note: almost stops just short, so the last letter is left off

parts.note: to close ranks is to unite

explanation.surface: A troop of soldiers nearly falls into tight formation.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a military formation, a group of troops organised to act together.

clue.text: Cattle drive

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a young castrated bullock
second meaning: to guide or direct, as a vehicle

explanation.walkthrough: Cattle drive reads as herding on the range; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A steer is a bullock raised for beef, and to steer is to guide the course of a car or ship.

clue.text: Left in a unit entirely without support?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: a unit is one, so a unit is a one
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A soldier abandoned in his unit with no backup at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone alone has nobody with them, so has no one to support them; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Go into battle to win some ground

definitions.meaning: first meaning: march out to begin fighting
second meaning, read literally: capture a piece of land

explanation.surface: An army goes to war to gain territory.
explanation.definitionFit: To take the field is the idiom for an army starting a campaign; read literally it means seizing a field.

clue.text: He raises unnecessary fears of a mistral storm

indicators.note: a storm throws things about wildly, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A forecaster frightens people needlessly about a coming mistral gale.
explanation.walkthrough: The mistral is a strong cold wind of southern France.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarmist is someone who spreads exaggerated warnings, causing needless panic.

clue.text: Faculty I mention in speech

indicators.note: in speech means as the words are said, not as they are spelt

parts.note: to mention is to cite, so I mention is I cite

explanation.surface: A university department I bring up in a lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: Faculty suggests a university department; it means one of the senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Sight is one of the five senses, and a sense is a faculty of the body.

clue.text: The final sentence

parts.note: surface reading: the last line of a piece of writing
setter's reading: a judge's sentence that ends a life, the last one anyone serves

explanation.walkthrough: Sentence pretends to be grammar; it is the punishment a court passes.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital punishment is the ultimate sentence a court can pass, final because nothing follows it.

clue.text: Issue a word of thanks for some music

parts.note: issue means offspring, such as a son
taken as written
ta is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: Releasing a note of gratitude to accompany a piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is a musical composition, typically for one or two instruments in several movements.

clue.text: Humourless nonsense, but it could bring the house down

definitions.text: it could bring the house down

parts.note: dry humour is deadpan, without levity
rot is rubbish, nonsense

explanation.surface: An unfunny show of drivel, which might yet bring the house down with laughter.
explanation.walkthrough: Bring the house down suggests a comedian's triumph; here it is a timber decay literally collapsing a building.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry rot is a fungus that destroys timber and can make a building structurally unsound until it collapses.

clue.text: They take one over water, or round a point

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so one piece goes around the next

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Ferries carry people across a lake or around a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Oars propel a rowing boat, so they carry a person across water.

clue.text: Less in sum perhaps

parts.note: surface reading: a smaller total, a lower amount
setter's reading: the word read aloud for the subtraction sign in an arithmetic sum

explanation.walkthrough: In arithmetic, seven less two is the same as seven take away two.
explanation.definitionFit: The word used for subtraction in a calculation means less, as in ten less three.

clue.text: Weapons kept up one's sleeve?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: firearms and other weaponry
second meaning, read literally: the limbs a sleeve covers

explanation.surface: Hidden guns, held in reserve like a card up a sleeve.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both weaponry and the upper limbs, which literally sit inside a person's sleeves.

clue.text: Break for an aspiring actor

parts.note: surface reading: a big chance, a breakthrough for a hopeful performer
setter's reading: the role itself, and also a verb meaning to separate

explanation.walkthrough: A break here is a lucky opportunity, which for an actor means being given a role.
explanation.definitionFit: A part is a role in a play, the opportunity a hopeful performer is waiting for, and to part is to break apart.

clue.text: Double act, no longer seen

parts.note: to do is to act
the doubling repeats the same short verb

explanation.surface: A comedy duo that has dropped out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: Double act suggests a pair of comedians; it means the verb do, twice.
explanation.definitionFit: The dodo is a flightless bird extinct since the 17th century, so it is never seen any more.

clue.text: Highly offensive actions

parts.note: surface reading: deeply insulting behaviour
setter's reading: attacks launched from high up in the sky

explanation.walkthrough: Offensive here means attacking, not rude, and highly means up in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombing raids by aircraft are attacks, offensive operations, carried out from great height.

clue.text: Acknowledging applause for violin playing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bending forward to an audience
second meaning: drawing a bow across the strings

explanation.surface: A soloist takes a bow at the end of a violin performance.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both stooping to thank a clapping audience and the stroke technique of a string player.

clue.text: One may be struck for showing off

definitions.text: One may be struck for showing off

parts.note: surface reading: someone gets hit as punishment for bragging
setter's reading: the idiom of striking a pose to impress

explanation.walkthrough: Struck suggests a blow, but the idiom is to strike a pose, adopting a theatrical posture.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike an attitude is to take up an affected bodily pose, done for effect or display.

clue.text: One flies to it via a small mountain

indicators.note: via means passing through, so one piece goes through the middle of the other

parts.note: taken as written
Mt is the short form of mount

explanation.surface: A traveller flies to a destination by way of a little hill.
explanation.walkthrough: One flies to it looks like a description of an airport; the definition is just One flies, a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The tomtit is a small bird, a common name for the blue tit or similar tits, and birds fly.
